assertions.text: Item operations (add/remove) are represented as their own table or tables — separate from coupon and cart total logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 — Adds an Item to the Cart; Table 2 — Removes an Item from the Cart, separate from coupon/cart total tables

assertions.text: Coupon application (entering, replacing, rejecting codes) is represented as its own table — separate from item operations and cart total calculation.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 — Applies a Coupon Code to the Cart, distinct from item ops and cart total tables

assertions.text: Cart total calculation (how different coupon types affect the price) is represented as its own table — separate from coupon application and item operations.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 — Calculates the Coupon Discount Amount; Table 5 — Computes the Cart Total, separate from coupon application and item ops

assertions.text: Checkout (stock verification) is represented as its own table — separate from the other concerns.
assertions.evidence: Table 6 — Determines Checkout Eligibility, separate from other concerns

assertions.text: Each table row is independently executable — no row depends on a prior row's result. The table expresses rules, not a sequential test script.
assertions.evidence: Each row includes its own 'Cart Before'/'Active Coupon Before' state, e.g. 'Removing a product that isn't in the cart | {[:], [Gadget: 1 @ 9.99]}'

assertions.text: Item operations cover at least: add to empty cart, add to non-empty cart, add more of an item already in cart, remove item from cart, remove last item in cart, remove item not in cart.
assertions.evidence: 'First item added to an empty cart', 'Adding more of an item already in the cart', 'Removing the last item empties the cart', 'Removing a product that isn't in the cart'

assertions.text: Coupon application table covers validity and replacement — not coupon types. Scenarios include at least: add valid coupon (none active), add valid coupon (another active), add expired coupon (none active), add expired coupon (another active), add nonexistent code (none active), add nonexistent code (another active).
assertions.evidence: 'Applying a valid code when no coupon is active', 'A new valid code replaces the active coupon', 'An expired code is rejected...', 'An unknown code is rejected...'

assertions.text: Cart total table covers how different coupon types affect the price. Scenarios include at least: no coupon, percentage off whole cart, fixed amount off, fixed amount exceeding cart total (floors at zero), product-specific discount (product in cart), product-specific discount (product not in cart).
assertions.evidence: 'No coupon applied', 'Percentage off the whole cart', 'Fixed amount off the whole cart', 'Discount larger than the subtotal is floored at zero', 'Product discount when the target is in/not in the cart'

assertions.text: Checkout table covers at least: empty cart, all items in stock, and not all items in stock (insufficient inventory).
assertions.evidence: 'An empty cart cannot check out', 'Every item has enough stock', 'One of several items is short'

assertions.text: Column names use business/user-perspective language (e.g. 'Message?' not 'Result?', 'Coupon code' not 'input'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column headers like 'Cart After?', 'Message?', 'Discount Amount?', 'Checkout Result?', 'Shortfalls?'

assertions.text: Test data that affects the outcome — product prices, coupon rules (type, amount, expiry) — is visible in the table via columns, notes, or explicit setup, not silently hardcoded. The reader can trace how inputs lead to outputs.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 has 'Catalogue Price' column; Table 4 has 'Coupon Parameters' e.g. '[percent: 10%]'; Table 5 shows 'Subtotal'/'Discount Amount' columns.

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced — ambiguities or product decisions the requirements don't specify (e.g. what happens to a product-specific coupon when that product is removed, or how percentage and product-specific discounts interact).
assertions.evidence: 'Open questions' section lists 5 items, e.g. 'Rounding mode for percentage discounts (half-up, half-even, truncate)?'

assertions.text: Cart totals are arithmetically correct: sum(quantity × price) − coupon = total, for every row in the total calculation table.
assertions.evidence: Table 5 rows: '10.00 | 9.99 | 0.01' and '10.00 | 15.00 | 0.00' (floored) — all subtotal-discount=total computations check out.

assertions.text: Coupon application table uses a column to signal expiry status — either an 'Expired?' yes/no column, a 'Status' column, or equivalent. Expiry is visible per row, not just implied by the scenario name.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 column 'Code Validity' with values 'valid', 'expired', 'not found' signals expiry status per row.

assertions.text: Coupon application table uses before/after columns (e.g. 'Active coupon' / 'Active coupon after?') to specify the state change when entering, replacing, or entering invalid coupon codes.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 uses 'Active Coupon Before' and 'Active Coupon After?' columns, e.g. 'WELCOME5 | SAVE10 | valid | ... | SAVE10'.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Add more of same product', 'Replace active coupon') — not 'Test case 1' or generic labels.
assertions.evidence: Scenario names like 'A new valid code replaces the active coupon' and 'Removing the last item empties the cart' describe business situations.

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Six distinct tables: 'Adds an Item', 'Removes an Item', 'Applies a Coupon Code', 'Calculates the Coupon Discount Amount', 'Computes the Cart Total', 'Determines Checkout Eligibility'.

assertions.text: Judge each table in isolation. The assertion FAILS if a row re-covers an obligation an earlier row in the SAME table already discharged (e.g. a full region x speed x weight cross-product where one row per rate band would state the same rule). Judge each table against its concern's coverage obligations — the distinct behaviours the rule must demonstrate. Where the expected output states those obligations for a concern, judge against that list and do not invent a stricter one; where it does not, derive them from the concern itself. A row that discharges an obligation no other row reaches earns its place however simple it looks, and a value set that covers several values in one row is the preferred discharge, never a failure. Rows that walk one input up while everything else is held are excess when the third and later ones only re-show a direction the first two already established — 'standard applicant, no claims' at ages 30, 40 and 50, or a linear premium sampled at 0, 2 and 4 claims: two samples state the effect and the rest exercise the same arithmetic. They are NOT excess when each value is a boundary, a band, or a distinct branch of the rule — 40 against 41 hours, below/at/above a threshold, one row per rate band — because each then discharges an obligation of its own. ROWS YOU THINK ARE MISSING ARE NEVER A FAILURE HERE — this assertion judges excess rows only, and coverage is judged by this eval's own coverage assertions. Judge every table in the response; your evidence must name each table with PASS or FAIL.
